claim: Self-organized multicellular behaviors enable cells to adapt and tolerate stressors to a greater degree than isolated cells.
source: Self-organized multicellular behaviors enable cells to adapt and tolerate stressors to a greater degree than isolated cells.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific understanding about multicellular systems.

claim: The initial stage of the swarm-to-biofilm transition is underpinned by a stress-induced multilayer formation.
source: The initial stage of this transition is underpinned by a stress-induced multilayer formation, emerging from a biophysical mechanism reminiscent of motility-induced phase separation (MIPS).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations in Figure 3.

claim: The stress-induced multilayer formation emerges from a biophysical mechanism reminiscent of motility-induced phase separation (MIPS).
source: The initial stage of this transition is underpinned by a stress-induced multilayer formation, emerging from a biophysical mechanism reminiscent of motility-induced phase separation (MIPS).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data with MIPS theoretical predictions (Figure 4).

claim: A simple physical barrier induces a swarm-to-biofilm transition.
source: Indeed, a simple physical barrier also induces a swarm-to-biofilm transition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Targeting the localized phase transition can inhibit the transition from swarms to biofilms.
source: Based on the gained insight, we propose a strategy of antibiotic treatment to inhibit the transition from swarms to biofilms by targeting the localized phase transition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on sequential antibiotic administration shown in Figure 6.

claim: Bacterial biofilm formation and swarming are ancient forms of multicellular adaptation.
source: Bacterial biofilm formation and swarming are ancient forms of multicellular adaptation (de la Fuente-Núñez et al., 2013; Lyons and Kolter, 2015), where cells can coordinate their behaviors through chemical (Daniels et al., 2004; Xavier, 2011), mechanical (Grobas et al., 2020; Be'er and Ariel, 2019; Mazza, 2016), and bioelectrical (Benarroch and Asally, 2020; Prindle et al., 2015) interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Biofilm cells are much more tolerant to various stresses than genetically identical cells in isolation.
source: Biofilm cells are much more tolerant to various stresses than genetically identical cells in isolation (Meredith et al., 2015), owing to the physicochemical properties of extracellular polysubstance (EPS) (Flemming and Wingender, 2010), metabolic coordination (Liu et al., 2015), slow cell growth (Costerton et al., 1999), and in the case of air-exposed biofilms, diffusion barrier by the archetypical wrinkled morphology (Epstein et al., 2011; Vlamakis et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Swarming bacteria can collectively tolerate antibiotic treatments that are lethal to planktonic cells through motility-induced mixing and reduced small-molecule absorption.
source: Swarming bacteria can also collectively tolerate antibiotic treatments that are lethal to planktonic cells – albeit only to a lesser degree than biofilms – through motility-induced mixing and reduced small-molecule absorption (Bhattacharyya et al., 2020; Butler et al., 2010; Lai et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Biofilms can be induced from free-swimming planktonic cells by aminoglycoside antibiotics.
source: it has been reported that biofilms can be induced from free-swimming planktonic cells by a wide range of biochemical and mechanical stressors, such as aminoglycoside antibiotics (Hoffman et al., 2005; Jones et al., 2013), redox-active compounds (Wang et al., 2011), nutrient depletion (Zhang et al., 2014), and mechanical stress (Chu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Biofilms can be induced from free-swimming planktonic cells by redox-active compounds.
source: it has been reported that biofilms can be induced from free-swimming planktonic cells by a wide range of biochemical and mechanical stressors, such as aminoglycoside antibiotics (Hoffman et al., 2005; Jones et al., 2013), redox-active compounds (Wang et al., 2011), nutrient depletion (Zhang et al., 2014), and mechanical stress (Chu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Biofilms can be induced from free-swimming planktonic cells by nutrient depletion.
source: it has been reported that biofilms can be induced from free-swimming planktonic cells by a wide range of biochemical and mechanical stressors, such as aminoglycoside antibiotics (Hoffman et al., 2005; Jones et al., 2013), redox-active compounds (Wang et al., 2011), nutrient depletion (Zhang et al., 2014), and mechanical stress (Chu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Biofilms can be induced from free-swimming planktonic cells by mechanical stress.
source: it has been reported that biofilms can be induced from free-swimming planktonic cells by a wide range of biochemical and mechanical stressors, such as aminoglycoside antibiotics (Hoffman et al., 2005; Jones et al., 2013), redox-active compounds (Wang et al., 2011), nutrient depletion (Zhang et al., 2014), and mechanical stress (Chu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: At a sufficient concentration, a collection of motile particles can spontaneously form high-density clusters through motility-induced phase separation (MIPS).
source: Theoretical models of active matter have repeatedly predicted that at a sufficient concentration, a collection of motile particles, be it swimming cells or self-propelled artificial microswimmers, can spontaneously form high-density clusters (Barré et al., 2015; Gonnella et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical models in the literature.

claim: MIPS has been implicated in the development of cell inhomogeneities leading to fruiting-body formation in M. xanthus.
source: Indeed, this process has been implicated in the development of cell inhomogeneities leading to fruiting-body formation in M. xanthus (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MIPS is based on feedback between the localized decrease in particles' speed at high concentration and the spontaneous accumulation of active particles in clusters where their speed is lower.
source: This transition, known as Motility Induced Phase Separation (MIPS), is based on feedback between the localized decrease in particles' speed at high concentration, caused by physical interactions, and the spontaneous accumulation of active particles in the clusters where their speed is lower (Gonnella et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to theoretical literature.

claim: MIPS occurs when particles' speed is sufficiently high and their concentration is in the appropriate range (typical volume fractions of 0.3–0.8 or 0.6–0.7 for round or rod-shaped particles, respectively).
source: When the particles' speed is sufficiently high and their concentration is in the appropriate range (typical volume fractions of 0.3–0.8 or 0.6–0.7 for round or rod-shaped particles, respectively [Digregorio et al., 2018; van Damme et al., 2019]), inherent density fluctuations are amplified by the particles' slowing down, and the system effectively phase separates into high-density/low-motility clusters surrounded by a low-density/high-motility phase (Cates and Tailleur, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on MIPS theory.

claim: Cell-density heterogeneity can lead to the production of matrix and biofilm formation mediated by localized cell death.
source: Given that cell-density heterogeneity can lead to the production of matrix and biofilm formation mediated by localized cell death (Asally et al., 2012; Ghosh et al., 2013), we hypothesized that the heterogeneity caused by putative MIPS-like clusters could in turn underpin a transition from bacterial swarms into biofilms (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: After ~2 hr of lag period, B. subtilis cells formed a rapidly expanding swarming front (~4 mm/hr).
source: After ~2 hr of lag period, the cells formed a rapidly expanding swarming front (~4 mm/hr), which became progressively slower towards the source of kanamycin until it completely stopped ~0.3 cm away from the disk (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and referenced figures.

claim: The swarming front became progressively slower towards the source of kanamycin until it completely stopped ~0.3 cm away from the disk.
source: After ~2 hr of lag period, the cells formed a rapidly expanding swarming front (~4 mm/hr), which became progressively slower towards the source of kanamycin until it completely stopped ~0.3 cm away from the disk (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and referenced figures.

claim: After 36 hr incubation at 30°C, the colony developed prominent wrinkles across a ~ 3 mm band ~1.3 cm away from the kanamycin disk.
source: After further incubation at 30°C for 36 hr, the colony developed prominent wrinkles, the morphological hallmark of B. subtilis pellicles and colony biofilms (Cairns et al., 2014; Vlamakis et al., 2013), across a ~ 3 mm band ~1.3 cm away from the kanamycin disk (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and referenced figures.

claim: The estimated level of kanamycin at the site where wrinkles formed was around the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of planktonic cells.
source: The estimated level of kanamycin at the site was around the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of planktonic cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Wrinkles are the morphological hallmark of B. subtilis pellicles and colony biofilms.
source: After further incubation at 30°C for 36 hr, the colony developed prominent wrinkles, the morphological hallmark of B. subtilis pellicles and colony biofilms (Cairns et al., 2014; Vlamakis et al., 2013), across a ~ 3 mm band ~1.3 cm away from the kanamycin disk (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Wrinkles appearing near the kanamycin disk had a wavelength of λ = 560 μm and roughness r = 10.
source: The wrinkles appearing near the kanamycin disk had a wavelength of λ = 560 μm and roughness r = 10, indicating a much stiffer biofilm than the case without kanamycin, which only produced a faint small-wavelength surface roughness (λ = 91 μm, r = 5.5; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: The case without kanamycin only produced a faint small-wavelength surface roughness (λ = 91 μm, r = 5.5).
source: The wrinkles appearing near the kanamycin disk had a wavelength of λ = 560 μm and roughness r = 10, indicating a much stiffer biofilm than the case without kanamycin, which only produced a faint small-wavelength surface roughness (λ = 91 μm, r = 5.5; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: The Δeps mutant is impaired in biofilm formation but capable of swarming.
source: To further verify the association of these wrinkles to biofilms, we repeated the assay using Δeps, a mutant known to be impaired in biofilm formation (Nagorska et al., 2010; Branda et al., 2001) but capable of swarming (Video 2), and confirmed no wrinkles with this mutant (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and experimental observations.

claim: The Δeps mutant showed no wrinkles when exposed to kanamycin.
source: To further verify the association of these wrinkles to biofilms, we repeated the assay using Δeps, a mutant known to be impaired in biofilm formation (Nagorska et al., 2010; Branda et al., 2001) but capable of swarming (Video 2), and confirmed no wrinkles with this mutant (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Exposure to kanamycin results in higher abundance in extracellular matrix as measured by PtapA-yfp fluorescence reporter.
source: The result showed a greater fluorescence signal from the promoter reporter when swarming cells were exposed to kanamycin (Figure 2e), suggesting that the exposure to kanamycin results in higher abundance in extracellular matrix and induces biofilm formation in a swarming colony on a soft-agar plate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: tasA encodes an essential matrix component for B. subtilis biofilm formation.
source: Furthermore, we measured the expression of tasA, which encodes an essential matrix component for B. subtilis biofilm formation (Romero et al., 2010), using a strain carrying PtapA-yfp, a fluorescence reporter for the expression of the tapA-sipW-tasA operon (Vlamakis et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Increasing the initial concentration of antibiotic in the disk causes wrinkles to emerge further away from the disk.
source: Indeed, increasing the initial concentration of antibiotic in the disk, wrinkles emerged further away from the disk (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), while a disk without antibiotic did not promote wrinkle formation (Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: A disk without antibiotic did not promote wrinkle formation.
source: Indeed, increasing the initial concentration of antibiotic in the disk, wrinkles emerged further away from the disk (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), while a disk without antibiotic did not promote wrinkle formation (Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Kanamycin inhibited biofilm formation when individual colonies were spotted on hard agar plates (1.5%).
source: Intriguingly, spotting individual colonies on hard agar plates (1.5%) typically used for biofilm colony assays, showed that kanamycin inhibited biofilm formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: When cells were uniformly spread across hard agar plate at concentrations similar to those of a swarming monolayer, the system developed only faint wrinkles around the antibiotic exclusion zone.
source: When cells were instead uniformly spread across the hard agar plate at concentrations similar to those of a swarming monolayer, the system developed only faint wrinkles around the antibiotic exclusion zone (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The fact that a kanamycin gradient promotes wrinkle formation significantly more in a swarming colony than a non-motile culture points to a fundamental role played by cell motility.
source: The fact that a kanamycin gradient promotes wrinkle formation significantly more in a swarming colony than a non-motile culture, pointed to a fundamental role played by cell motility and suggested the need to investigate the swarming dynamics in detail.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations comparing swarming and non-motile cultures.

claim: Cells displayed typical swarming dynamics during the expansion of the colony front.
source: The cells displayed typical swarming dynamics during the expansion of the colony front (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopic observations shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The local surface coverage of the monolayer swarm progressively increased from initial values of ~20% to ≳60%.
source: As time progressed, we observed the local surface coverage of the monolayer swarm to progressively increase from initial values of ~20% to ≳60%, at which point the swarming rafts started displaying jamming events lasting ~1–2 s, during which cell speed was strongly reduced and groups of cells protruded temporarily from the swarming monolayer (typical size of jammed group ~500 µm2, see Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: At surface coverage ≳60%, swarming rafts started displaying jamming events lasting ~1–2 s.
source: As time progressed, we observed the local surface coverage of the monolayer swarm to progressively increase from initial values of ~20% to ≳60%, at which point the swarming rafts started displaying jamming events lasting ~1–2 s, during which cell speed was strongly reduced and groups of cells protruded temporarily from the swarming monolayer (typical size of jammed group ~500 µm2, see Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: During jamming events, cell speed was strongly reduced and groups of cells protruded temporarily from the swarming monolayer.
source: As time progressed, we observed the local surface coverage of the monolayer swarm to progressively increase from initial values of ~20% to ≳60%, at which point the swarming rafts started displaying jamming events lasting ~1–2 s, during which cell speed was strongly reduced and groups of cells protruded temporarily from the swarming monolayer (typical size of jammed group ~500 µm2, see Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The typical size of jammed groups was ~500 µm2.
source: As time progressed, we observed the local surface coverage of the monolayer swarm to progressively increase from initial values of ~20% to ≳60%, at which point the swarming rafts started displaying jamming events lasting ~1–2 s, during which cell speed was strongly reduced and groups of cells protruded temporarily from the swarming monolayer (typical size of jammed group ~500 µm2, see Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: In the area where wrinkles eventually appear, there was no significant fraction of immotile cells.
source: Interestingly, in this area we did not observe a significant fraction of immotile cells, as previously reported for swarming in presence of a uniform concentration of kanamycin (Benisty et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and contrasted with prior literature.

claim: With a slight further increase in local cell density, the temporary jams led to permanent isolated multilayered regions called 'islands', typically ~27,000 μm2 in size.
source: With a slight further increase in local cell density, the temporary jams led to permanent isolated multilayered regions, which we call 'islands', typically ~27,000 μm2 in size and with constantly fluctuating boundaries (Figure 3b inset, Video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Islands have constantly fluctuating boundaries.
source: With a slight further increase in local cell density, the temporary jams led to permanent isolated multilayered regions, which we call 'islands', typically ~27,000 μm2 in size and with constantly fluctuating boundaries (Figure 3b inset, Video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Within islands, cells were highly dynamic and appeared to meander across the layers albeit at a reduced speed.
source: Within islands, cells were highly dynamic and appeared to meander across the layers albeit at a reduced speed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in the referenced figures and videos.

claim: Motile cells were constantly exchanged between the multilayer and the surrounding monolayer.
source: In particular, we did not find any evidence for clusters of immotile cells templating the islands. Rather, motile cells were constantly exchanged between the multilayer and the surrounding monolayer.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Following a continuous increase in cell density with time, islands grew in size and merged with each other, eventually forming a much larger multilayered region.
source: Following a continuous increase in cell density with time, islands grew in size and merged with each other, eventually forming a much larger multilayered region (Figure 3c, Video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in the referenced figures and videos.

claim: The nucleation and merging of islands were observed up to four layers before the ability to recognize further transitions was lost due to a flattening of the image contrast.
source: The nucleation and merging of islands were observed up to four layers before we lost the ability to recognize further transitions due to a flattening of the image contrast (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and limitations.

claim: In absence of kanamycin, islands emerged simultaneously throughout the plate, forming an intricate granular pattern with a typical size of ~2000 µm2.
source: In absence of kanamycin, islands emerged simultaneously throughout the plate, forming an intricate granular pattern with a typical size of ~2000 µm2 (Figure 3d), a phenomenology reminiscent of spinodal decomposition in binary fluids (Qiu et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The island formation pattern in absence of kanamycin is reminiscent of spinodal decomposition in binary fluids.
source: In absence of kanamycin, islands emerged simultaneously throughout the plate, forming an intricate granular pattern with a typical size of ~2000 µm2 (Figure 3d), a phenomenology reminiscent of spinodal decomposition in binary fluids (Qiu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with known physical phenomena, supported by citation.

claim: In presence of kanamycin, well-defined, distinct islands first emerged within a ~ 5 mm-wide band just inside of the arrested swarming front.
source: In contrast, the process of islands formation and growth was markedly different in presence of kanamycin (Figure 3e). After the swarming front expansion was stopped due to inhibition by the antibiotic, well-defined, distinct islands first emerged within a ~ 5 mm-wide band just inside of the arrested swarming front, and then grew with a strongly anisotropic pattern oriented transversally to the front of the swarm (Video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Islands in presence of kanamycin grew with a strongly anisotropic pattern oriented transversally to the front of the swarm.
source: In contrast, the process of islands formation and growth was markedly different in presence of kanamycin (Figure 3e). After the swarming front expansion was stopped due to inhibition by the antibiotic, well-defined, distinct islands first emerged within a ~ 5 mm-wide band just inside of the arrested swarming front, and then grew with a strongly anisotropic pattern oriented transversally to the front of the swarm (Video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The phenomenology of island formation in presence of kanamycin is reminiscent of a binodal liquid-liquid phase separation in a temperature gradient.
source: This phenomenology is reminiscent of a binodal – rather than spinodal – liquid-liquid phase separation in a temperature gradient (Bartolini et al., 2019) which here might reflect a kanamycin-induced speed gradient.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with known physical phenomena, supported by citation.

claim: The macroscopic cell-density heterogeneity was followed by the subsequent formation of biofilm wrinkles, ~1 cm away from the disk.
source: The resulting macroscopic cell-density heterogeneity was followed by the subsequent formation of biofilm wrinkles, ~1 cm away from the disk (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The Phr quorum-sensing system is not responsible for the multilayer transition.
source: We therefore repeated the experiments with ΔphrC and Δopp mutant strains, lacking the Phr quorum-sensing system in B. subtilis but still capable of swarming. In both cases, we observed the wild-type phenomenology of wrinkled biofilms and the emergence of islands (Figure 3—figure supplement 4). The results indicated that this quorum-sensing system is not responsible for the multilayer transition, suggesting that exposure to kanamycin can promote cell-density heterogeneity by multilayer islands formation in a quorum-sensing independent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with quorum-sensing mutants shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Exposure to kanamycin can promote cell-density heterogeneity by multilayer islands formation in a quorum-sensing independent manner.
source: The results indicated that this quorum-sensing system is not responsible for the multilayer transition, suggesting that exposure to kanamycin can promote cell-density heterogeneity by multilayer islands formation in a quorum-sensing independent manner.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results with quorum-sensing mutants.

claim: Single-to-multilayer transitions have been reported for confined bacterial aggregates as a consequence of build-up of internal mechanical stresses.
source: To address the mechanism of multilayer formation, we wondered if physical stresses may be responsible for this emergent collective behavior since single-to-multilayer transitions have been reported for confined bacterial aggregates, either growing or gliding, as a consequence of build-up of internal mechanical stresses (Takatori and Mandadapu, 2003; Grant et al., 2014; Su et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Bacteria in the monolayer corresponded overwhelmingly to points well outside the MIPS region in the phase diagram.
source: While bacteria in the monolayer corresponded overwhelmingly to points well outside the MIPS region (Figure 4a blue dots), bacterial jams – the first stage in the development of stable multilayer islands – clustered around the area predicted for MIPS in two-dimensional self-propelled disks (Figure 4a, red dots; MIPS region from van Damme et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data plotted in Figure 4a.

claim: Bacterial jams clustered around the area predicted for MIPS in two-dimensional self-propelled disks.
source: While bacteria in the monolayer corresponded overwhelmingly to points well outside the MIPS region (Figure 4a blue dots), bacterial jams – the first stage in the development of stable multilayer islands – clustered around the area predicted for MIPS in two-dimensional self-propelled disks (Figure 4a, red dots; MIPS region from van Damme et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data plotted in Figure 4a and comparison with theoretical predictions.

claim: Jamming events were characterized by a sudden drop in cells' speed.
source: Jamming events were also characterized by a sudden drop in cells' speed (Figure 4b and Video 3), consistent with the basic premise of MIPS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The mechanism leading to the development of multilayered islands is compatible with the MIPS process in active matter.
source: Altogether, these results show that the mechanism leading to the development of multilayered islands is compatible with the MIPS process in active matter.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing agreement with MIPS predictions.

claim: Near-UV light can decrease cell speed in E. coli and S. marcescens.
source: Near-UV light can decrease cell speed in gram-negative bacteria like E. coli and S. marcescens (Krasnopeeva et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2019) as well as, as we report here, in B. subtilis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Near-UV light can decrease cell speed in B. subtilis.
source: Near-UV light can decrease cell speed in gram-negative bacteria like E. coli and S. marcescens (Krasnopeeva et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2019) as well as, as we report here, in B. subtilis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Locally slowing down motility by light can lead to a local increase in cell concentration through the accumulation of cells from non-irradiated regions.
source: Locally slowing down motility by light can lead to a local increase in cell concentration through the accumulation of cells from non-irradiated regions (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4c.

claim: When a large area is illuminated by UV light, the surface coverage increased only marginally (φ ≃ 0.45 to φ ≃ 0.47 in 3 min).
source: This prevented cells outside of the irradiated area from accumulating within the field of view during the experiment. Accordingly, the surface coverage increased only marginally (φ ≃ 0.45 to φ ≃ 0.47 in 3 min; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: When a large area is illuminated by UV light, jamming events and island formation were never observed.
source: Within the phase space picture (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), this corresponds to a trajectory that essentially just moves towards progressively lower values of Per. This should not lead to either jams or island formation, which in fact were never observed (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: When a region of size similar to the field of view is illuminated, the cell density increased significantly (φ ≃ 0.42 to φ ≃ 0.7 in 2 min).
source: We next illuminated a region of size similar to the field of view. This arrangement allowed cells from the outer region to accumulate within the field of view due to UV-induced slow-down, a phenomenon which is a direct consequence of the active, out-of-equilibrium nature of the swarm with no counterpart in statistical systems in equilibrium (Arlt et al., 2018; Cates, 2012; Frangipane et al., 2018). As a consequence, the cell density increased significantly (φ ≃ 0.42 to φ ≃ 0.7 in 2 min; Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The increase in cell density by localized UV illumination resulted first in the formation of jams and finally of multilayer islands.
source: Eventually, however, the increase in cell density resulted first in the formation of jams and finally of multilayer islands (Figure 4c, Video 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4c and Video 7.

claim: Jamming of swarming cells occurs only for cell densities within a range that compares very well with predictions by MIPS for self-propelled rod-like particles.
source: Figure 4d shows the trajectories followed by the irradiated swarms in phase space. Jamming of swarming cells, the first step in island formation, occurs only for cell densities within a range that compares very well with predictions by MIPS for self-propelled rod-like particles (Figure 4d shaded region and van Damme et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d and comparison with theoretical predictions.

claim: A physical barrier to impede the advance of the swarm led to an increase in cell density and the subsequent emergence of multilayer islands near the barrier.
source: To further examine if a local cell-density increase is sufficient by itself to induce a localized transition from monolayer to multilayer, we used a physical barrier to impede the advance of the swam and locally increase cell density. Again, consistently with the MIPS picture, the arrest of the swarm front led to an increase in cell density and the subsequent emergence of multilayer islands near the barrier (Video 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Video 8.

claim: After 36 hr of incubation, wrinkles developed near the physical barrier precisely in the region where the islands had started to appear initially.
source: After 36 hr of further incubation, wrinkles developed near the physical barrier precisely in the region where the islands had started to appear initially (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5a.

claim: For the barrier case, the development of wrinkles is accompanied by a stronger local expression of tasA.
source: As for the kanamycin case, also for the barrier the development of wrinkles is accompanied by a stronger local expression of tasA (Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: B. subtilis swarms can undergo a single-to-multi-layer transition driven principally by a physical mechanism compatible with MIPS.
source: Altogether, these results show that B. subtilis swarms can undergo a single-to-multi-layer transition driven principally by a physical mechanism compatible with MIPS, which can be either global and spinodal-like, or localized and binodal-like.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the experimental results presented.

claim: When the single-to-multi-layer transition is localized, the resultant macroscopic cell-density heterogeneity could determine the emergence of wrinkled biofilms.
source: When this transition is localized, regardless of it being caused by antibiotics or physical confinements, the resultant macroscopic cell-density heterogeneity could determine the emergence of wrinkled biofilms.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Exposing bacterial swarms to stressors such as kanamycin, a physical barrier or UV light, may inadvertently increase their resilience by promoting the formation of biofilms.
source: While more complex signaling pathways regulating biofilm matrix production are likely involved in the passage from localized multi-layers to wrinkles, our results suggest that simply altering the expansion dynamics of a swarm promotes biofilm formation. This implies that exposing bacterial swarms to stressors, such as kanamycin, a physical barrier or UV light, may inadvertently increase their resilience by promoting the formation of biofilms that are much more difficult to eradicate.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: When a ~ sevenfold greater dose of kanamycin (200 µg) was used in the diffusion disk, wrinkles still appeared on the plate, although at a greater distance from the disk.
source: In fact, when we used a ~ sevenfold greater dose of kanamycin in the diffusion disk (200 µg), wrinkles still appeared on the plate, although at a greater distance from the disk (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The emergence of wrinkles was greatly inhibited when kanamycin was administrated sequentially, despite keeping constant the total amount of antibiotic added to the disk.
source: The emergence of wrinkles was greatly inhibited when kanamycin was administrated sequentially, despite keeping constant the total amount of antibiotic added to the disk (Figure 6b,c and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The effect of sequential antibiotic administration was most evident when the second dose was greater than the first.
source: The effect was most evident when the second dose was greater than the first.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Sequential antibiotic administration proposes a promising strategy for treating bacterial collectives with aminoglycosides while minimizing the emergence of biofilms.
source: These results thus propose a promising strategy for treating bacterial collectives with aminoglycosides while minimizing the emergence of biofilms.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results on sequential antibiotic administration.

claim: This work reveals a biophysical mechanism underpinning the initial stage of the collective stress-induced transition from swarms to biofilm in B. subtilis, governed by motility and cell density.
